exhibit.title: Bounded ping result
exhibit.text:
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos; timeout 2 seconds:
.!!!!
Success rate: 80 percent (4/5)

prompt: What does this ping result establish?
options: The destination enforced a four-reply ICMP limit for this source.
One request did not receive a reply within its wait; the cause needs more evidence.
A routing update installed the route immediately after the first request.
The first request was definitely discarded during ARP resolution.
explanation: The period reports a timeout and the four exclamation marks report replies. ARP startup delay is one possible explanation; repeat the test and correlate a current ARP/capture observation before assigning that cause.

whyWrong.0: Four replies do not establish a configured response limit.
whyWrong.3: The output contains no ARP observation.

exhibit.title: Ping response characters
exhibit.text:
R1# ping 10.0.50.1
U.U.U
Success rate: 0 percent

prompt: What conclusion follows from the U characters?
options: Destination-unreachable responses were reported for some probes.
The source router had no usable interface for every probe.
The destination application accepted and then closed its connections.
Each period proves a fixed 500-ms ICMP response limiter on R2.
explanation: U indicates unreachable evidence, unlike a period indicating a wait expired. Inspect the ICMP source and code, then routing/policy, rather than infer one device or a fixed rate limiter from the pattern.

whyWrong.1: The display does not establish all interfaces were unusable.
whyWrong.2: Echo testing does not create an application connection.
whyWrong.3: The pattern alone supplies neither the timer nor its location.

prompt: Which two statements correctly compare conventional IOS traceroute and Windows tracert? Select two.
options: IOS normally uses ICMP echo while Windows normally uses UDP.
Windows tracert normally uses ICMP echo requests.
IOS normally uses UDP probes toward high destination ports.
Both tools must use the same probe transport to discover any hops.
explanation: Both use increasing TTL to obtain transit time-exceeded responses. Their probe protocols differ, which matters when comparing source and policy paths.

whyWrong.0: This reverses the conventional implementations described here.
whyWrong.3: Different probe transports can elicit TTL-expiry responses; their policies may differ.

prompt: Which two statements about these tables are accurate? Select two.
options: An absent ARP entry proves the host has never received a neighbor reply.
A dynamic MAC entry identifies a VLAN/port that learned that source MAC.
An incomplete ARP entry shows resolution is incomplete at this observation.
A learned MAC establishes the host has the correct mask and gateway.
explanation: The tables describe different current mappings. Aging, clearing, and recent traffic affect their contents; neither alone certifies host addressing or all historical communication.

whyWrong.0: Entries can age or be cleared after earlier successful communication.
whyWrong.3: MAC learning does not inspect the host mask/gateway as proof of correctness.

exhibit.title: Routed Ethernet state
exhibit.text: Gi0/1 10.0.99.1 YES manual down down

prompt: On this routed Ethernet interface, what should be investigated first?
options: Remove a local shutdown command, which this status explicitly proves.
Change the IP mask before checking whether either end has carrier.
Replace the cable immediately because down/down uniquely proves its failure.
Inspect local media and the connected peer's current link state.
explanation: Down/down directs attention to physical/link availability and the peer. It does not uniquely identify a cable defect; a local shutdown normally has the distinct administratively-down status.

whyWrong.0: A local shutdown normally has the distinct administratively-down state.
whyWrong.1: The IP mask does not restore physical link detection.
whyWrong.2: The peer may be disabled or unpowered; this display does not isolate the cable.

exhibit.title: Both-end duplex and current counters
exhibit.text:
SW1 Fa0/24: 100 Mb/s, half duplex; late collisions rose 40→65
R1 Gi0/0: speed 100; duplex full

prompt: Which demonstrated problem should be corrected before further performance testing?
options: Late collisions establish damaged copper regardless of the peer settings.
The displayed half/full settings establish a duplex mismatch.
The rising late collisions measure output-queue congestion.
The two 100-Mb/s values establish a negotiated speed mismatch.
explanation: Half duplex at SW1 and full duplex at R1 establishes a mismatch. Coordinate matching supported settings at both ends, then compare new error increments; clean CRC alone does not certify media.

whyWrong.0: The configuration directly establishes duplex disagreement; the counter alone cannot isolate copper damage.
whyWrong.2: Late collisions are not output-queue drops.
whyWrong.3: Both displayed speeds match at 100 Mb/s.

exhibit.title: Trace with a silent intermediate hop

prompt: A web application is slow. Which interpretation of this trace is justified?
options: The destination replies certify that HTTP performance is normal.
The three stars establish three seconds of forwarding delay for each user packet.
The third router dropped every packet and caused the slow application.
Later probes received replies, so the middle stars alone do not prove a forwarding break.
explanation: A star is a missing probe response within the wait. Later replies weaken the claim of a complete path break, but load sharing, response policy, and application behavior still require investigation.

whyWrong.0: Traceroute does not test the HTTP transaction.
whyWrong.1: A response timeout is not a measurement of per-packet forwarding delay.
whyWrong.2: Later responses contradict an assertion that all traffic necessarily stops there.

exhibit.title: Logging threshold and two messages
exhibit.text:
logging trap warnings
%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Gi0/1 changed state to down
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Gi0/1 line protocol changed state to down

prompt: Which shown message is eligible for remote syslog at the configured threshold?
options: Neither message is selected because warnings means exactly severity 4.
Only the severity-5 LINEPROTO message is selected by this threshold.
Both messages are selected because both concern the same interface.
Only the severity-3 LINK message is selected by this threshold.
explanation: Warnings admits severity 4 and lower-numbered, more severe messages. This selects the severity-3 message; actual receipt still requires a working logging path.

whyWrong.0: The threshold includes more severe levels, not just exact level 4.
whyWrong.1: Severity 5 is less severe than the configured level 4 threshold.
whyWrong.2: Each message is filtered by its own severity.

prompt: What does this client-side TCP observation support?
options: A matching reset was received; identify the generating endpoint or intermediary before attributing the refusal.
The reset proves the client cannot receive any packet from that direction.
The SYN was silently discarded and no response reached the client.
The capture alone proves the application server itself generated the reset.
explanation: The reset is an active response, unlike silence. A firewall or intermediary can generate resets using the endpoint address, so correlate server-side capture and service status before declaring the server process at fault.

whyWrong.1: The reset itself arrived from that direction.
whyWrong.2: The matching RST is an observed response.
whyWrong.3: The observed source address alone does not exclude an intermediary.

exhibit.title: Received ICMP error
exhibit.text:
10.0.99.2 → 10.0.10.50
ICMP Destination Unreachable: communication administratively prohibited (type 3, code 13)

prompt: Which next check is supported by the received ICMP error?
options: Replace the missing default route that this code uniquely identifies.
Correct the expired TTL that is explicitly reported in this message.
Inspect administrative forwarding policy at the reporting device and the matching flow.
Repair ARP for the destination because this is a host-unreachable code.
explanation: Type 3 code 13 reports administrative prohibition. It supports investigating policy, but does not identify one exact ACL line without further configuration/counter evidence.

whyWrong.0: No-route evidence would be a different unreachable reason.
whyWrong.1: TTL expiry uses time-exceeded rather than this administrative prohibition.
whyWrong.3: Host unreachable is a different code.

prompt: On supporting IOS, which bounded command compares a 1500-byte IPv4 datagram with the path MTU?
options: ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1500 df-bit
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1472
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 100 df-bit
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1500
explanation: IOS size specifies the datagram size in this command and df-bit prevents fragmentation. A received fragmentation-needed error is informative; a timeout alone does not prove the MTU value.

whyWrong.1: That requests a different IOS datagram size, not 1500.
whyWrong.2: A 100-byte datagram does not perform the requested large-size comparison.
whyWrong.3: Without DF, IPv4 fragmentation can occur.

exhibit.title: Two independent switch-port conditions
exhibit.text:
Fa0/3: err-disabled
Fa0/4: inactive, configured access VLAN 30
show vlan brief: VLAN 30 absent

prompt: The design requires VLAN 30 on Fa0/4. Which action pair follows the supplied evidence?
options: Move both ports to an existing VLAN without checking their intended subnets.
Replace both cables before inspecting the recorded state and VLAN database.
Inspect Fa0/3's protection cause and restore the intended VLAN 30 for Fa0/4.
Enable Fa0/3 without checking why its protection acted.
explanation: Err-disabled requires its recorded cause and corrective action before controlled recovery. The explicit VLAN inventory identifies the missing intended VLAN for Fa0/4; do not move clients into an unrelated network.

whyWrong.0: That changes the documented VLAN design without repairing its missing object.
whyWrong.1: The two displayed conditions do not establish physical cable damage.
whyWrong.3: Recovery without resolving the triggering cause can repeat the failure.

prompt: Which statement describes errors during the measured interval?
options: There were 900 new CRC errors during this transfer.
The retained total proves that the present cable must be replaced.
The 2,000,000 packets prove that no loss occurred elsewhere.
No new CRC errors were counted on this interface during the interval.
explanation: The CRC counter remained 900, so its delta is zero. Preserve that distinction between history and this test; a clean delta on one interface is not an end-to-end certification.

whyWrong.0: Nine hundred is the retained total, not the difference.
whyWrong.1: The retained count lacks evidence of a current cable fault.
whyWrong.2: One receive count cannot prove delivery across the whole path.

exhibit.title: Counters bracketing one controlled transfer
exhibit.text:
Same interface; no counter clear or reboot.
Before: 1,000,000 input packets; 900 CRC
After: 3,000,000 input packets; 900 CRC

prompt: What should the investigation focus on next for this transaction?
options: Inspect the responding application and its dependencies for the reported failure.
Change the client resolver and repeat the same lookup before examining the service.
Add a host route to the approved server to repair the unsuccessful request.
Raise the TCP connection timeout and retry before checking the service response.
explanation: The completed connection and received application response prove more than a ping. The service reports temporary unavailability for this request; investigate that service and its dependencies without declaring unrelated traffic healthy.

whyWrong.1: The observed lookup already returned the approved address.
whyWrong.2: A complete TCP exchange and HTTP response do not justify this route change.
whyWrong.3: The request received an explicit response; this is not an uncompleted TCP connection attempt.

exhibit.title: One captured application transaction
exhibit.text:
Intended name resolves to the approved IPv4 address.
TCP SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK complete for that address.
HTTP response to the request: 503 Service Unavailable.

prompt: Which evidence is still required before closing the incident?
options: A repeat of R1's successful directly connected peer ping.
A screenshot showing the exact intended configuration line.
A fresh original-service test from the affected client.
An updated uptime display after restarting the router.
explanation: A route change and router test do not cover the affected client's whole path or application. Retest its original service and record the source, destination/name, result and any remaining limitation.

whyWrong.0: The local router test exercises a narrower path.
whyWrong.1: Configuration shows intent, not successful delivery.
whyWrong.3: A restart is not an acceptance test and may erase useful evidence.

exhibit.title: Repair acceptance record
exhibit.text:
Original complaint: PC-A cannot load the named application.
A missing route was restored.
R1 can ping the server.
No PC-A application test has been repeated.

exhibit.title: Same DHCP attempt at two capture points
exhibit.text:
Server-side: relayed Discover received; Offer sent to giaddr 10.0.10.1
Client-side: Discover transmitted; no Offer observed in the same interval

prompt: Which conclusion is justified by these captures from the same fresh DHCP attempt?
options: Investigate delivery of the Offer from the server through the relay to the client.
The client certainly received the ACK but lost its default gateway setting.
The helper must be absent because no server reply can exist without it.
The server certainly had no matching pool and never constructed an Offer.
explanation: The server-side observation shows an outgoing Offer while the client-side view does not show receipt. Narrow the investigation to return and relay delivery, including capture coverage; do not assert a unique fault yet.

whyWrong.2: A forwarded Discover and outgoing reply have already been observed.
whyWrong.3: An outgoing Offer contradicts the claim that none was constructed.

prompt: Which follow-up preserves the useful distinction between the two probe results?
options: Treat the error as evidence of a size constraint; inspect the reported MTU and a smaller DF probe.
Treat both tests as proof that the server is down at every packet size.
Replace DNS settings because a larger numeric-address probe cannot resolve the name.
Remove DF and call the original unfragmented-size requirement verified if a reply arrives.
explanation: A received fragmentation-needed error positively reports a constraint for that DF packet. Correlate its source and any next-hop MTU value, then compare a smaller packet with the same source and destination; fragmentation-permitted success answers a different question.

whyWrong.1: The smaller probe already received replies.
whyWrong.2: The test already uses a numeric address.
whyWrong.3: Fragmented delivery does not verify the original unfragmented requirement.

exhibit.title: Controlled IPv4 size comparison
exhibit.text:
Same source and destination, ordinary 20-byte IPv4 header.
100-byte DF datagrams receive replies.
1500-byte DF datagrams receive ICMP fragmentation-needed errors.
No numeric next-hop MTU has yet been read.

prompt: Which incident note is defensible before comparing these event times?
options: R2 must have caused R1's event because its printed time is earlier.
Record each clock's uncertainty and correlate a shared observation before ordering the events.
Use the collector's arrival order as proof of the devices' event order.
Subtract the displayed times and report a measured propagation delay.
explanation: Different unverified clocks do not provide a reliable cross-device timeline. Preserve their original text and obtain synchronization/offset or a shared observation before asserting which event preceded the other.

whyWrong.0: Printed times on unverified clocks do not establish causality.
whyWrong.2: Collection paths and buffering can change arrival order.
whyWrong.3: The difference includes unknown clock offsets.

exhibit.title: Log times from two devices
exhibit.text:
R1: *10:15:01 link event; clock not authoritative
R2: 10:14:58 neighbor event; synchronization not checked
Collector receives R1's message first.

prompt: Which narrow next action fits the remaining failure?
options: Undo the route repair and return to investigating the original missing route.
Correct the stale DNS record, then test a fresh answer and the named application.
Clear only the client DNS cache and close the incident after a numeric-address test.
Assign the server the stale address .99 to avoid changing the DNS service.
explanation: The restored numeric-address service and fresh wrong answer identify a separate DNS-data problem. Preserve both findings and validate the original name-based service after correcting the record.

whyWrong.0: The repaired path now carries the numeric-address service, and the DNS data shows a separate fault.
whyWrong.2: A fresh direct response from the resolver is already wrong; a client cache clear does not repair that configured record.
whyWrong.3: The approved server remains .10, so renumbering it to match stale DNS changes the design unnecessarily.

exhibit.title: Checks after a routing repair
exhibit.text:
Approved server: 10.31.20.10.
PC-A HTTP to 10.31.20.10 now succeeds.
Fresh direct query to its intended resolver: app.lab.example A = 10.31.20.99.
The DNS configuration confirms that stale address; .99 is unused.

prompt: Which two conclusions are supported before a repair is chosen? Choose two.
options: This interface has counted new outgoing drops during the interval.
The clean CRC count certifies every cable in the network.
Raising a buffer limit would guarantee recovery without any further evidence.
The switch must have a duplex mismatch despite both endpoints showing full.
The displayed queue evidence is relevant to local egress congestion.
explanation: Current outgoing drops and a full egress queue point toward congestion at this observation point. They do not uniquely identify its source, prescribe one fix, or certify the rest of the path.

whyWrong.1: A clean receive counter on one interface does not certify all media.
whyWrong.2: Traffic demand, scheduling and downstream capacity still matter.

exhibit.title: Current egress observations
exhibit.text:
During one test: output drops 50→150.
Receive CRC unchanged at 0.
Both endpoints operate full duplex.
The egress queue reaches its configured limit during the test.

exhibit.title: Tests with different source addresses
exhibit.text:
R1 source 10.0.99.1 → 10.0.20.10: success
R1 source 10.0.10.1 → 10.0.20.10: failure
PC-A 10.0.10.50/24: local gateway ping succeeds

prompt: R1 can ping the server from its transit source, but not from its LAN source. What should the engineer check next?
options: Retest from the transit source and close the issue if it succeeds again.
Add another R1 route to the server subnet before checking the reply destination.
Inspect the server return routes and source-dependent policy for the LAN source.
Replace the PC access cable, then repeat only the router-source test.
explanation: Changing the source changes the return destination and may change policy handling. The failed sourced test supports investigating those differences; it does not alone prove a missing route.

whyWrong.0: The transit source does not test replies toward the failed LAN source.
whyWrong.1: The successful transit-source test and changed reply destination call for return/policy investigation before another forward-route change.
whyWrong.3: The failed router-originated LAN-source test does not traverse the PC access cable.

prompt: Which next measurement best tests whether the observed capture gap is actual path loss?
options: Count the analyzer warnings and report that count as packets lost on the server link.
Run a short ping after the transfer and use its loss percentage as the TCP loss rate.
Capture a different successful flow and use that result to dismiss the original gaps.
Compare a complete capture at a second point for the same flow and interval.
explanation: The analyzer reports what its captured sequence history lacks. The capture itself dropped packets, so corroborate the same flow elsewhere before attributing loss to a network link.

whyWrong.0: The capture dropped packets itself, so missing sequence history does not count losses on an identified network link.
whyWrong.1: A later ICMP sample is not the same TCP flow or observation interval.
whyWrong.2: A different flow may take different treatment and does not corroborate the missing sequence history.

exhibit.title: Capture coverage and application evidence
exhibit.text:
Client transfer completes, but intermittently slowly.
Capture tool reports dropped capture packets.
Wireshark labels a gap: Previous segment not captured.
No second capture or current interface counter interval is available.

prompt: Which next check most directly separates a wrong server return next hop from a forward-path failure?
options: Install another R2 route to the client subnet before examining the server route.
Inspect the server's selected route and neighbor resolution for the client reply.
Ping the server from R2 and treat that reply as proof of the client return path.
Capture the client gateway ARP exchange again before examining reply forwarding.
explanation: The server-side capture confirms the tested request arrived. Its route and selected next-hop resolution are now useful discriminators for the missing reply; the capture alone does not establish whether the application generated one.

whyWrong.0: A matching R2 return route is already supplied; the server next-hop choice is the missing dependency under investigation.
whyWrong.2: A reply to R2 uses a different destination and does not settle how the server returns to the client.
whyWrong.3: The request reached the server, so the unresolved return next hop is more directly discriminating here.

exhibit.title: Matched observations for one attempt
exhibit.text:
Client 10.31.10.50 sends to server 10.31.20.10.
Server capture sees that request. Client capture sees no reply.
Server is /24; its route/default-gateway configuration has not been inspected.
R2 route to 10.31.10.0/24 is present.

prompt: What is the most useful next test for the original client failure?
options: Capture only R1-originated replies and use them to clear the client access path.
Repeat the router-source service test until five successive attempts pass.
Compare client-source policy and the client-facing ingress path.
Increase the client's retry timeout before comparing how its flow is handled.
explanation: The router-source test does not traverse the client-facing ingress path and uses a different source address. Compare the actual client flow and both policy directions before concluding the paths are equivalent.

whyWrong.0: Router-originated replies do not establish treatment of the actual client source or ingress.
whyWrong.1: Repeated router tests still omit client ingress and use a different source.
whyWrong.3: The supplied source/path difference deserves investigation before changing a client timer.

exhibit.title: Different-origin test paths
exhibit.text:
PC-A reaches its gateway but cannot reach a remote service.
R1 reaches that service with source set to its LAN interface address.
PC-A's address, mask and gateway match the plan.
Client-source policy and ingress handling have not been checked.
